Abstract.AbstractText: Nowadays, studies of the interactions of DNA with small molecular drugs, especially anti-tumor agents, antibiotics and drugs of abuse are currently performed to explore their mechanism of action and develop new drugs with lower side effects and high curative properties. Currently, electrochemical biosensors are considered a very promising alternative analytical tool to conventional more complex techniques for drug determination due to rapidness, low cost, high sensitivity, compatibility with microfabrication technology, intuitively understandable design and simple operation mode. Although most electrochemical biosensors reported so far for drugs determination rely on the interactions between the drug of interest and DNA (both in solution or at DNA-modified electrodes), other interesting approaches have been proposed also based on monitoring the DNA damage and the use of aptamers and specific DNA-protein interactions. Different strategies have been employed for electrochemical detection of DNA-drug interaction: recording oxidation of guanine (and to a less extent adenine) residues in the DNA strand, detecting signal referred to electrochemically active drug or diffusion-free markers which change their electrochemical characteristics in reaction with DNA, and monitoring changes in the surface layer morphology followed by alteration of its permeability and charge transfer resistance. In this review, selected electrochemical nucleic acid-based biosensing methods described so far for drug determination are briefly overviewed by discussing the basics and main features of chosen examples. Moreover, a section pointing out general conclusions and future directions in this field is also provided.
